title: Unlabeled Modal Close Button
desc: Close button on all modal dialogs lacks a programmatically identified label that describes the purpose of the control. i.e. "Close"
rem: Change markup and apply a descriptive label that is programmatically associated with the control. This can be remediated multiple ways, including the label element. Other options include use of the title attribute and aria-label which are used to directly provide text that is used for the accessibility name, or aria-labelledby which indicates an association with other text on the page that is providing the name. Button controls can have a name assigned in other ways but in certain situations may require use of label, title, aria-label, or aria-labelledby.

title: No Focus Management
desc: When the modal is opened, focus is not set to the new content. Focusable components must receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. When focus is not set to the start of new content, users of assistive technology may lose context requiring backwards movement in reading/focus order.
rem: Edit markup so that when modals appear, focus is set to the start of new content or first focusable control, whichever comes first. If focus must be set to a non-controllable element which normally does not receive focus, such as headings, use tabindex="-1" so that the element becomes tabbable but does not exist in the regular tab order as this would be unexpected behavior. Keep user focus within the modal until the modal is closed and then return focus to the triggering element.

title: Poor Focus Indicator
desc: Controls lack an adequate visible focus indicator when in keyboard focus, making it difficult for users to determine which element currently has focus.
rem: Ensure all keyboard focusable controls have a contrasting visible focus indicator when in keyboard focus. Update design and/or styles so that all controls meet or exceed the required contrast ratio of 3:1 for non-text content. By default, all native HTML controls should have a visible focus indicator across all browsers. Either revert controls to make use of native elements or update design and/or styles so that all custom keyboard focusable controls are provided a contrasting visible focus indicator when in keyboard focus.

title: No Visible Focus
desc: Controls do not display a visible focus indicator when navigated using the keyboard. Users are unable to visually identify which element currently has keyboard focus.
rem: Ensure that all keyboard-focusable elements display a visible focus indicator when they receive focus. Provide a focus style that is clearly distinguishable from surrounding content and remains visible while the element is focused. Avoid removing default browser focus outlines unless an accessible custom focus style is provided.

title: Keyboard Inaccessible
desc: Controls are not keyboard accessible — they cannot be focused or activated using keyboard only. All controls must be focusable and operable with keyboard control.
rem: Update markup so that all controls are keyboard focusable and actionable. They must also include a contrasting, visible focus indicator.

title: Keyboard Inaccessible, Missing Roles
desc: This defect is two distinct issues that have been combined with the intention that they share a common solution. 1. The controls are not keyboard accessible despite being clickable. 2. The controls do not have programmatically identifiable roles. When custom UI elements/controls are created, additional measures must be taken to ensure that the controls provide important and appropriate information and allow themselves to be controlled by assistive technologies. Additionally, there must be a contrasting visible focus indicator when these issues are resolved.
rem: 1. Update markup so that all controls are keyboard focusable and actionable. 2. This issue can be remediated multiple ways. The primary way is to choose elements that are inherently focusable controls, such as buttons, that can also have accessible names (labels) applied to them. Generic elements such as div and span do not have any predefined roles. When these generic elements are used to create UI controls in HTML the assistive technology may not have the necessary information to describe and interact with the control. Other solutions may include use of ARIA but only if absolutely necessary. The controls must also include a contrasting, visible focus indicator.

title: Insufficient Text Contrast
desc: Text falls below the required contrast ratio of 4.5:1 against its background, making it difficult or impossible to read for users with low vision or color vision deficiencies.
rem: Adjust color value of text, background, or both so that they have a text contrast ratio of 4.5:1 or greater.

title: Insufficient Non-text Contrast
desc: Non-text elements such as icons, form input borders, and UI component boundaries fall below the required contrast ratio of 3:1 against adjacent colors. Users with low visual acuity may have difficulty identifying and interacting with elements that fall below the required contrast.
rem: Update element design/styles so that they have a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater against adjacent colors.

title: Poor, Missing, or Unnecessary Alt Text
desc: Images have alt text that is missing, non-descriptive, or duplicates adjacent visible text. Alt text should describe the purpose of the image, not necessarily the image itself.
rem: Determine if an image is decorative or informative (content). Ensure all informative elements have short, descriptive alternate text and all decorative elements have empty alt attributes (e.g. alt="") or are hidden from assistive technology through another means. Ensure that screen text does not duplicate alt text.

title: Unlabeled Control
desc: A control does not have a programmatically identified accessible name. Users of assistive technology are unable to determine the purpose of the control when it receives focus.
rem: Change markup and apply a descriptive label that is programmatically associated with the control. This can be remediated multiple ways, including the label element. Other options include use of the title attribute and aria-label which are used to directly provide text for the accessibility name, or aria-labelledby which indicates an association with other text on the page that is providing the name.

title: No Skip Link
desc: There is no mechanism available to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple pages, such as a typical "Skip to Main Content" link.
rem: Update markup and design to add a skip link ahead of repetitive content that is visible when focused and appropriately changes a user's focus when activated.

title: Visually Inaccessible Skip Link
desc: A skip link is present but is not visible to sighted keyboard users. Skip links are utilized by keyboard-only users and should be visible when focused.
rem: Ensure that skip links are visible when focused by the user. The link should become visible when it receives keyboard focus, so that sighted keyboard users are also able to benefit from it.

title: Heading-Like Text Not Properly Marked Up
desc: Heading-like text is not marked up as headings. If text is used to denote the start of a content section — generally styled visually to be larger or bolder than regular body text — then it must be marked up as a heading.
rem: Update markup so that visible headings which denote the start of a content section have an appropriately applied role. This is usually accomplished by choosing an appropriate heading level element.

title: No Heading Level One Present
desc: There is no heading level one <h1> present on the page.
rem: Update markup accordingly so that each page has at least one <h1> and the heading level increments by one according to the content.

title: Heading Hierarchy
desc: Heading levels increase by more than one. Ensure headings follow a logical order. Check that all headings are marked h1 through h6 and ordered hierarchically. Do not use heading markup on text that isn't truly a heading that introduces content.
rem: Update markup templates accordingly so that each page has at least one <h1> and the heading level increments by one according to content.

title: Undefined Asterisk
desc: Form inputs use asterisks to denote required form fields but the meaning of the asterisk is not defined. It is important that the asterisk meaning is defined at the start of the form.
rem: Define any symbols meant to convey meaning, including asterisks denoting required form fields. Ensure that required form fields are also programmatically identified.

title: Inadequate Error Identification
desc: Form errors should be programmatically associated with the input field in which they refer. When errors appear on screen they should set focus to the first form control which has an error.
rem: Ensure that error messages are associated with the relevant form field using a technique such as aria-describedby. Set keyboard focus to the first form field in error.

title: No Status Message
desc: When new content appears or an action is completed, no status message is programmatically conveyed to assistive technology. Users of assistive technology are not informed that a change has taken place.
rem: Choose and implement a sufficient technique for widely conveying status message updates to users whenever new content appears in response to user actions. Status messages should be programmatically determined through role or properties such that they can be presented to users by assistive technology without receiving focus. Acceptable methods include role="status" or aria-live. Avoid use of aria-live="assertive" or ARIA alerts unless the status is time-sensitive in nature.

title: Improper ARIA Usage
desc: When navigating between pages or sections, a change of content is announced through use of role="alert" which should be reserved for important, time-sensitive status messages due to its intrusive nature.
rem: Implement a new method for properly setting focus and communicating updated status messages to screen reader users. A typical method for accomplishing this is to set focus when routing to a new page on to a persistent and consistent element such as an <h1>.

title: Invalid ARIA
desc: Elements marked with aria-hidden, such as those used in this component, must not be focusable or contain focusable elements. Using the aria-hidden="true" attribute on an element removes the element and ALL of its child nodes from the accessibility API making it completely inaccessible to screen readers and other assistive technologies.
rem: Correct markup to remove implementation of unnecessary or invalid ARIA. Remove the misapplied aria-hidden attribute. If aria-hidden is used to hide visible content from screen readers, the identical or equivalent meaning and functionality must be exposed to assistive technologies.

title: Sole Use of Color
desc: Color is used as the only means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element. This information is not available to users who cannot perceive color differences.
rem: Update design and markup so that color is not the only means of conveying information. Add a supplemental visual indicator such as an underline, icon, pattern, or text label. Ensure that any programmatic state changes are also conveyed to assistive technology.

title: Zooming and Scaling Disabled
desc: The user-scalable="no" parameter inside the content attribute of <meta name="viewport"> element disables zooming on the page. The maximum-scale parameter limits the amount the user can zoom. This is problematic for people with low vision who rely on screen magnifiers to properly see the contents of a web page.
rem: Remove the user-scalable="no" parameter from the content attribute of the <meta name="viewport"> element in order to allow zooming and ensure the maximum-scale parameter is not less than 2.

title: No Visible Label
desc: All form controls, such as input fields, should have a visible label or equivalent. Placeholders should not be used as labels. All labels must also be programmatically associated to the fields in which they refer.
rem: Modify markup and provide every form control a visible and programmatically associated <label>. Alternative methods include aria-label or aria-labelledby.

title: No Label Association
desc: Input fields lack a programmatically associated label. Form input elements must have labels that are both visible and programmatically associated.
rem: Update markup so that all form controls have programmatically associated labels. The most common method is to use the label element and an explicit association using the for and id attributes. The aria-label attribute may be acceptable to use under certain circumstances. Placeholders are not sufficient form labels.

title: Improperly Hidden Content
desc: Before hidden content is opened, or after it is closed, it is not adequately hidden from users of assistive technology and can still be read and seemingly interacted with.
rem: If content is intended to be hidden from users, it must also be hidden from users of assistive technology. Correct markup to properly hide content from users of assistive technology. This can be achieved a number of ways, such as CSS display:none; or aria-hidden.

title: Inadequate Text Spacing
desc: Letter, word, and line spacing was observed not meeting the required standard. This could be difficult for users to read and understand the content being conveyed.
rem: Modify styles so that text letter, word, lines, and paragraphs are all adequately spaced from one another and meet or exceed minimum WCAG SC: line height to at least 1.5 times the font size; spacing following paragraphs to at least 2 times the font size; letter spacing to at least 0.12 times the font size; word spacing to at least 0.16 times the font size.

title: Label in Name
desc: An aria-label is used to customize the screen reader output in a way that does not match the visible text label. When visible labels and accessible names do not match, speech-input users may not be able to navigate by speaking the visible text labels of the component. It is not advisable to manipulate the accessible name to force screen readers to output in a specific way since individual user software and settings and actual output cannot be determined.
rem: Remove the aria-label which customizes the output for screen readers. Ensure the control's visible text label and accessible name match.

title: ARIA Tabs
desc: This component uses ARIA tabs which are known to be problematic as they necessitate unexpected keyboard behavior requiring use of arrow keys in an unexpected context. It is better to simplify with different elements as ARIA tabs are prone to breakage and overengineering.
rem: Update markup to achieve the same or similar functionality without reliance on ARIA tabs.

title: Tabbable Non-Control
desc: An element is tabbable despite not being interactive or a control. Using tabindex on a non-interactive element, such as a div, can obstruct use of assistive technology and confuse users. Only interactive elements should appear in the tab order, catering preference to elements which are inherently tabbable controls and don't require tabindex. i.e. button, input, textarea.
rem: Correct markup and remove the tabindex attribute.

title: Redundant Adjacent Controls
desc: Content blocks contain multiple links that point to the same destination — the image, the text description, and a CTA are all separate controls. For a keyboard user, it is tedious to navigate through redundant links. For users of assistive technologies, it can be confusing to encounter successive identical links.
rem: Correct markup so that there is no repeated content or controls. Consider wrapping all into a single focusable element or marking the image as decorative and allowing the text to serve as the link.

title: Language of Parts
desc: Language changes on the page but this is not programmatically communicated. When a page contains content in more than one language, the language of each passage or phrase must be programmatically determinable.
rem: Update markup so that any changes in language on a page are indicated using the lang attribute on the element containing the passage or phrase in a different language.

title: Missing Lang Attribute
desc: The html element is missing the lang attribute with an appropriate value. Without this, screen readers may not be able to determine the language of the page and may use the wrong pronunciation rules.
rem: Add a lang attribute to the html element (e.g. <html lang="en">) whose value represents the primary language of the document. Apply to all pages. Update lang attribute value as needed.

title: Dragging Movement
desc: Dragging functionality is not apparently accessible to keyboard-only users. At full viewport width, controls may be visible but serve no keyboard-accessible function.
rem: Correct markup to supplement dragging behavior with keyboard-accessible controls.

title: Continuous Animation
desc: An animated element begins animation automatically and loops indefinitely with no mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it.
rem: Update markup/design so that any animation that starts automatically either resolves within five seconds or provides the user with a clear and accessible mechanism to pause, stop, or hide the animation. Ensure any controls used to manage animation are keyboard accessible and clearly labeled.

title: No Landmarks
desc: All page content should be contained within landmarks, with one main landmark. Without landmarks, users of assistive technology are unable to orient themselves to the page or navigate between sections efficiently.
rem: Make markup changes to ensure all content is contained within a landmark region, designated with HTML5 landmark elements and/or ARIA landmark regions.

title: Poor Landmark and Content Structure
desc: Ensure that all content on the page is contained within a landmark region. Landmarks programmatically identify sections of a page and help assistive technology users orient themselves and navigate easily to various sections.
rem: Update markup to utilize HTML sectioning elements such as header, footer, main, aside, nav, etc. If this is not possible, apply ARIA landmark roles to mark page sections. All contents excepting skip links should be contained within landmarks.

title: Static Title
desc: The page title does not change between screens or pages. Page titles must be accurate, informative, and adequately describe the page so that users can distinguish different pages.
rem: Ensure page title changes on each screen or page. Page titles must be accurate, informative, and adequately describe the page so that users can distinguish different pages.

title: Keyboard Trap
desc: Keyboard focus becomes trapped within a component. Once keyboard focus is moved to this component, it is not possible to move focus away using only a keyboard interface.
rem: Update markup so that keyboard users do not become stuck when navigating controls through tabbing or other means. Ensure all interactive elements allow keyboard focus to move in and out using standard key interactions.

title: Inaccessible Data Visualization
desc: Charts and graphs are inaccessible outside of their visible, graphical format. The data and insights they convey are not available to users of assistive technology.
rem: Formulate a strategy and choose an appropriate non-text replacement for data contained within the data visualization. A text alternative with a longer description should identify the type of chart, provide a high-level summary of the data, trends, or implications comparable to those available from the chart. Where possible and practical, the actual data should be provided in a table.

title: Tabular Data Not in Table
desc: Tabular data is presented without using semantic table markup. Without proper table structure, the relationships between headers and data cells are not programmatically conveyed, making the content difficult for users of assistive technologies to navigate and understand.
rem: Update the markup so that comparison or tabular data is presented using a proper programmatic table structure, including appropriate table, row, and header elements. Ensure header cells are correctly associated with their corresponding data cells.

title: Content on Hover
scLabel: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
desc: Content appears only on pointer hover and is not accessible by keyboard or accessible to assistive technology users. If pointer hover can trigger additional content, that content must also be keyboard accessible and must persist until dismissed.
rem: Correct markup so that all helpful or necessary content or content changes are not limited to mouse access. Ensure the tooltip or hover content is also triggered by keyboard focus, can be dismissed without moving focus, and persists until the user moves focus away.

title: Unlabeled Form Inputs
desc: Form fields and other controls are missing discrete visible labels. The placeholder field alone is not sufficient as a programmatically associated label.
rem: Update design and markup to ensure that all form fields and controls are given descriptive labels both visually and programmatically so that users can identify the purpose of the inputs.

title: Poor or Missing Focus Order
desc: The focus/tab order of the interface does not follow the visible order. An assistive technology user may have trouble predicting where focus will go next when the source order does not match the visual order.
rem: Update markup or design so that focus order matches visible order. Avoid using positive tabindex values to manipulate focus order, and ensure that the source order reflects the intended reading and navigation order.

title: Poorly Labeled Control
desc: Some controls have poor accessible names that describe the visual appearance of the control rather than its purpose or function. Accessible names for images and controls should describe the purpose instead of the image itself.
rem: Determine the function or destination of a control (links, buttons) and apply a label that correctly identifies this for users of assistive technology. i.e. Change labels like "Search icon" to "Search".

title: Inaccessible Content
desc: Content that conveys information visually is hidden from users of assistive technology. The information conveyed by this content is not available through any programmatic means.
rem: Remove the aria-hidden attribute from informative content and replace with appropriate accessible names or text alternatives. Alternatively, add supplemental text which conveys the same content i.e. "Rating: 5 stars".

title: No New Window Warning
desc: No warning or messaging is provided before a link or control opens in a new window or tab. This can be disorienting for users who do not expect a change in context.
rem: The name or label that describes a control can include a warning about opening in a new window. Update the link text or accessible name to indicate that activating the link will open in a new window or tab.

title: Change on Focus
desc: When a component receives focus, it initiates a change of context. When any UI component receives focus, it should not initiate a change on focus.
rem: Update markup and/or design so that receiving focus does not initiate an unexpected change of context. If a change of context is required, ensure the user is advised of this behavior before using the component.

title: Change on Input
desc: Changing the setting of a user interface component automatically causes a change of context. Selecting one of the options causes a change of context such as a page reload or loss of keyboard focus.
rem: Correct form functionality to prevent the change on input. One technique could utilize a submit button to initiate the change rather than doing so upon selection.

title: ARIA Alert on Blur
desc: ARIA alerts are used for errors which should be reserved for important, time-sensitive status messages due to their intrusive nature.
rem: Consider alternate use of aria-live rather than role="alert" for communicating error messages.

title: Inaccurate Content
desc: Content is formatted in such a way where its meaning would not be programmatically conveyed accurately to assistive technology. For example, price formatting or broken content structure causes incorrect announcements.
rem: Correct markup so that the content is accurately conveyed to users of assistive technology.
